questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Terminating and repeating decimals
questions.learningObjective: recognise a decimal expansion that terminates
questions.stem: Which of these decimal expansions stops after a finite number of digits instead of repeating forever?

options.text: 0.375, because after three decimal places there is nothing new to write
0.333 with more 3 digits continuing forever, because the digit 3 never stops
options.misconception: believes a long run of one digit is a finished decimal

options.text: 0.2727 repeated, because a block of two digits is short enough to end
options.misconception: believes a short repeating block must eventually stop on its own

options.text: 0.1010 repeated, because the two digits differ from each other
options.misconception: believes alternating digits are the sign of a terminating decimal

questions.explanation: A decimal expansion terminates when it can be written with a whole number of thousandths and no digits after that. The value 0.375 is exactly 375 thousandths, so it ends there. The other three all settle into a repeating block that runs on forever, which is the mark of a rational number whose reduced denominator carries a prime factor other than 2 or 5.
questions.hint: Look for the one that runs out of digits.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Repeating decimal to a fraction
questions.learningObjective: convert a repeating decimal to a fraction in lowest terms
questions.stem: Four labelled steps describe turning the repeating decimal 0.7777 into a fraction in lowest terms. Put them in the order in which they must be carried out.

options.text: Subtract the two equations so the infinite repeating tails cancel and whole numbers remain
Reduce the resulting fraction to lowest terms
Rewrite the number as a fraction whose denominator is 99, since a repeat of one digit gives nine
Call the number x and multiply by 10 so one copy of the repeating block shifts left

questions.explanation: Letting the number equal x and multiplying by 10 shifts one whole repeating block to the left so the tails line up. The shortcut is that a one digit repeat puts 9 in the denominator, which here gives 77 over 99. Subtracting then cancels the tails and leaves 9x equal to 7, and only afterwards is the fraction reduced.
questions.hint: The tails must line up before anything can cancel.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: A repeating decimal equal to one
questions.learningObjective: explain why an endless tail of nines equals 1
questions.stem: A display rounds to 0.999 and so on, yet the number is actually equal to 1. Why is that so?

options.text: The repeating 9 fills the whole gap up to 1, so the value is exactly 1
The value is 0.99, a separate number sitting just below 1
options.misconception: believes an endless tail of nines always falls short of the next whole number

options.text: The value is 0.9, because only the first digit after the point counts
options.misconception: believes a repeating block collapses to its first digit

options.text: The value has no expansion at all, because a repeating pattern is not a number
options.misconception: denies that an endless decimal can name a real value

questions.explanation: Call the number x, multiply by 10 so the tails line up, and subtract. The tails cancel and leave 9x equal to 9, so x equals 1. The digit 9 is the only one that carries forever without a gap, which is why its endless tail reaches the next whole number instead of falling short of it.
questions.hint: Multiply by 10, subtract, and see what is left over.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: A terminating decimal in lowest terms
questions.learningObjective: write a terminating decimal as a fraction in lowest terms
questions.stem: The decimal 0.8125 is written as a fraction p over q in lowest terms. What is the value of q? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Four decimal places means four thousandths, so 0.8125 equals 8125 over 10000. Dividing top and bottom by 625 gives 13 over 16, and 13 and 16 share no factor, so the fraction is in lowest terms. The check is that 16 carries only the primes 2 and 5, which is exactly what lets a decimal terminate.
questions.hint: Four decimal places gives thousandths, then reduce.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Prime factor test for a terminating decimal
questions.learningObjective: apply the prime factor test to a denominator
questions.stem: A fraction is in lowest terms. Which condition on its denominator guarantees that its decimal expansion terminates?

options.text: The denominator has no prime factors besides 2 and 5
The denominator has no prime factors besides 2, 3 and 5
options.misconception: believes a factor of 3 is still allowed because single digits are small

options.text: The denominator has no prime factors besides 3 and 7
options.misconception: believes the primes in the denominator are the ones that appear in the digits

options.text: The denominator has no prime factors at all, so it must equal 1
options.misconception: believes a denominator free of prime factors is always possible

questions.explanation: A denominator built only from 2s and 5s can be cleared by multiplying by enough tens, because each 2 pairs with a 5 to make a 10. Any other prime factor, such as 3 or 7, survives and forces the expansion to repeat. This is why one half stops but one third does not.
questions.hint: Think about which primes can be paired into tens.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Reducing a fraction to lowest terms
questions.learningObjective: reduce a fraction and report the reduced pair
questions.stem: The fraction 84 over 126 is rewritten in lowest terms as p over q. What is the value of p plus q? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The largest common factor of 84 and 126 is 42, and dividing both parts by it gives 2 over 3. The prime forms make the factor easy: 84 is 2 squared times 3 times 7, while 126 is 2 times 3 squared times 7, so the shared part is 2 times 3 times 7. The reduced parts are 2 and 3, which add to 5.
questions.hint: Factor both parts, then cancel what they share.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Common denominator for two fractions
questions.learningObjective: find the common denominator needed to add fractions
questions.stem: The fractions 5 over 8 and 3 over 12 are to be added. What is the smallest positive common denominator that must be used? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: A common denominator must be a multiple of both 8 and 12, and the smallest such number is 24, since 8 divides 24 three times and 12 divides 24 twice. Writing 5 over 8 as 15 over 24 and 3 over 12 as 6 over 24 is what finally lets the numerators be added, because like denominators are the precondition for adding numerators at all.
questions.hint: Find the smallest number both 8 and 12 divide into.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Adding two fractions with unlike denominators
questions.learningObjective: add two fractions with unlike denominators
questions.stem: Adding 3 over 4 and 5 over 6 gives a fraction a over b in lowest terms. What is the value of a plus b? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The common denominator of 4 and 6 is 12, so 3 over 4 becomes 9 twelfths and 5 over 6 becomes 10 twelfths, giving 19 twelfths. Since 19 is prime and 12 is not, nothing cancels, so the parts are 19 and 12 and they add to 31. The common denominator step is the whole job, because unlike numerators cannot be added as they stand.
questions.hint: Scale both fractions up to twelfths first.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Clearing a denominator in a complex fraction
questions.learningObjective: explain why multiplying top and bottom keeps a fraction equal
questions.stem: A complex fraction has 3 over 4 as its numerator and 1 over 8 as its denominator. What does multiplying the top and the bottom of the whole expression by 8 accomplish?

options.text: It clears the smaller denominator and leaves a fraction of the same value
It doubles the value, because two denominators have been combined
options.misconception: believes clearing a denominator scales the value along with it

options.text: It converts the fraction into a decimal approximation
options.misconception: believes multiplying by a whole number is a form of rounding

options.text: It turns the fraction into a whole number, since 8 is a multiple of 4
options.misconception: believes any multiple of the denominator cancels the numerator away

questions.explanation: Multiplying the top and the bottom of any fraction by the same nonzero value leaves it equal, because the extra factor appears once above the bar and once below. Here the top becomes 3 times 8, which is 24, and the bottom becomes 4 times 8, which is 32, so 24 over 32 is still 3 over 4 in disguise. Only the appearance changes, never the value.
questions.hint: Whatever you multiply by must go on both sides of the bar.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Simplifying a complex fraction
questions.learningObjective: simplify a complex fraction and report the reduced pair
questions.stem: The complex fraction with numerator 2 over 3 plus 1 over 6 and denominator 1 over 2 simplifies to a over b in lowest terms. What is the value of a plus b? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: First the top: 2 over 3 is 4 sixths, and 4 sixths plus 1 sixth is 5 sixths. Then dividing by 1 over 2 means multiplying by the reciprocal 2, giving 10 sixths, which is 5 thirds. The parts 5 and 3 share no factor, so they add to 8. Dividing by a fraction is the step most often mistaken for multiplying, which would halve the value instead.
questions.hint: Simplify the top, then multiply by the reciprocal of the bottom.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Using a ratio to split a total
questions.learningObjective: split a total in a given ratio
questions.stem: In a class of 36 pupils the ratio of girls to boys is 5 to 4. How many girls are there? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The ratio 5 to 4 has 9 parts in total, and those 9 parts account for all 36 pupils, so one part is 36 divided by 9, which is 4. The girls take 5 of the parts, giving 5 times 4, which is 20. The boys take the remaining 4 parts, which is 16, and 20 plus 16 returns the total of 36 as a check that the split was right.
questions.hint: Add the parts, then find what one part is worth.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: What a proportion asserts
questions.learningObjective: state what equality of two ratios means
questions.stem: A proportion is built from two ratios. What does it assert about those two ratios?

options.text: The ratios are equal, so cross multiplying gives an equation to solve
The ratios are close to each other, so rounding is good enough
options.misconception: believes a proportion only asks two ratios to be near one another

options.text: The ratios are reciprocals, so their products equal 1
options.misconception: believes a proportion pairs a ratio with its reciprocal

options.text: The ratios are opposites, so one is subtracted from the other
options.misconception: believes a proportion states the two ratios are negatives

questions.explanation: A proportion says one ratio equals another, and that single statement is an equation in disguise. Writing a over b equals c over d and multiplying across gives a times d equal to c times b, a linear equation in one unknown. That is the whole reason proportions are useful: a relationship phrased as two rates becomes something you can solve for an unknown part.
questions.hint: Think about what equal ratios let you do algebraically.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solving a proportion for one part
questions.learningObjective: solve a proportion for the unknown part
questions.stem: A proportion states that 3 is to 5 as x is to 20. Which value of x satisfies it?

options.text: 12, because 20 multiplied by 3 over 5 is 12
20, because the two matching parts must be equal
options.misconception: believes a proportion forces the matching parts to be the same number

options.text: 33 and one third, because 20 multiplied by 5 over 3 is larger
options.misconception: inverts the ratio instead of keeping the given correspondence

options.text: 9, because 20 multiplied by 3 over 4 is 9
options.misconception: adjusts the ratio to a different pair of numbers before scaling

questions.explanation: Writing 3 over 5 equals x over 20 and cross multiplying gives 3 times 20 equal to 5 times x, so 60 equals 5x and x is 12. The check is the ratio itself: 12 over 20 reduces to 3 over 5, exactly matching the given pair. Doubling both 3 and 5 leaves the ratio at 6 to 10, confirming the factor was chosen correctly.
questions.hint: Cross multiply, then divide by the coefficient.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Reading a rate from two measurements
questions.learningObjective: compute a rate from distance and time
questions.stem: A car covers 288 kilometres in 4 hours at a steady speed. Which rate describes the motion?

options.text: 72 kilometres per hour, because 288 divided by 4 is 72
1152 kilometres per hour, because distance is multiplied by time
options.misconception: multiplies the two measurements instead of dividing to reach a rate

options.text: 18 kilometres per hour, because time is divided by distance
options.misconception: divides the distance by the time the wrong way round

options.text: 4 kilometres per hour, because the hours are the fixed quantity
options.misconception: treats the second measurement as the size of the rate itself

questions.explanation: A rate is one quantity measured against another, so the 288 kilometres is divided by the 4 hours to give kilometres per hour, which is 72. The units confirm it, because the kilometres cancel while the hours stay in the denominator. Checking back, 72 kilometres per hour for 4 hours returns the original 288 kilometres.
questions.hint: Divide the first measurement by the second, then check the units.

questions.topic: Using a unit rate to price an amount
questions.learningObjective: use a unit rate to find a cost for a given quantity
questions.stem: A store prices paint at 27 dollars for 6 litres. What is the cost in dollars of 14 litres at the same rate?

options.text: 63 dollars, because 14 multiplied by 27 over 6 is 63
37 dollars, because 14 multiplied by 6 over 27 is smaller
options.misconception: divides by the unit price instead of multiplying price by quantity

options.text: 78 dollars, because 14 multiplied by 27 is the total before dividing
options.misconception: forgets to scale down to the price of a single litre

options.text: 4.5 dollars, because 27 divided by 6 prices a whole order
options.misconception: reports the unit rate itself rather than the price for the amount asked

questions.explanation: The unit rate is 27 dollars divided by 6 litres, which is 4.5 dollars for each litre, and 14 litres at 4.5 dollars is 63. The second route agrees, because 14 over 6 is 2 and one third and 27 dollars multiplied by 2 and one third is 63 dollars. Finding the unit rate is what turns the problem into a single multiplication.
questions.hint: Find the price of one unit, then multiply by the amount needed.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Writing a percent as a decimal
questions.learningObjective: convert a percent to a decimal
questions.stem: Which decimal carries the same value as the percent 62%?

options.text: 0.62, because the percent sign means out of every hundred
6.2, because the percent sign means multiplied by 100
options.misconception: believes the percent sign scales the number up instead of down

options.text: 0.062, because the percent sign means out of every thousand
options.misconception: believes a percent is measured per thousand rather than per hundred

options.text: 62.0, because the percent sign only marks the unit
options.misconception: believes the number is unchanged and the sign is decoration

questions.explanation: Per cent literally means per one hundred, so 62% asks for 62 hundredths, and 62 hundredths is 0.62. Dividing by 100 moves the point two places to the left, which is the same operation. The reverse direction multiplies by 100 and moves the point two places to the right, so 0.04 becomes 4%.
questions.hint: Divide by 100 and count the places.

questions.topic: A decimal read as a percent
questions.learningObjective: convert a decimal to a percent
questions.stem: A fraction of a shipment is recorded as the decimal 0.375. What percent does that decimal represent?

options.text: 37.5 percent, because multiplying 0.375 by 100 gives 37.5
3.75 percent, because the point moves one place not two
options.misconception: moves the decimal point one place instead of two places

options.text: 375 percent, because the percent sign means times one thousand
options.misconception: believes per cent means per thousand when converting upwards

options.text: 0.375 percent, because a decimal cannot be read as a percent
options.misconception: believes a decimal is a different kind of number from a percent

questions.explanation: A percent is a number of hundredths, so turning a decimal into a percent means multiplying by 100, shifting the point two places right: 0.375 becomes 37.5. The check runs the other way, since 37.5 percent of 200 items is 75 items and 0.375 of 200 is also 75 items, so the two readings agree on a real quantity.
questions.hint: Multiply by 100 and count the places.

questions.topic: Base used by a percent increase
questions.learningObjective: identify the base of a percent increase
questions.stem: A price of 80 dollars is increased by 15%. Which amount is the increase, and what base was used?

options.text: 12 dollars, found by taking 0.15 of the original 80 dollars
13.80 dollars, found by taking 0.15 of the new 92 dollar price
options.misconception: uses the price after the increase as the base for the increase

options.text: 15 dollars, found by taking the rate itself against the base
options.misconception: believes the percent number is already the amount of the change

options.text: 12 dollars, found by taking 0.85 of the original 80 dollar price
options.misconception: uses the complement of the rate and describes the same total as the increase

questions.explanation: A percent increase is defined against the amount that existed before the change, so 0.15 of 80 dollars is 12 dollars and the new price is 92. Option B uses the value after the change, which double counts the increase, and option D uses 0.85, which is the new price rather than the change. The increase is always 0.15 of the original 80 dollars.
questions.hint: Ask what the amount was before anything changed.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Successive percent changes compounding
questions.learningObjective: apply a rise and a fall in sequence
questions.stem: A price of 200 dollars is raised by 15% and then, on the new price, reduced by 15%. What is the final price in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The rise gives 200 multiplied by 1.15, which is 230 dollars, and the fall then gives 230 multiplied by 0.85, which is 195.5 dollars. The two factors together are 1.15 times 0.85, equal to 0.9775, so the price ends at 97.75% of where it started. The two changes do not cancel, because the second percentage acts on a larger base than the first did.
questions.hint: Work the first change, then use its result as the base for the second.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Percent change from an old and a new value
questions.learningObjective: compute a percent change from two recorded values
questions.stem: A town records 6400 residents in one year and 8000 residents the next. What is the percent increase, and which value is the base?

options.text: 25 percent, because 1600 divided by the original 6400 is 0.25
20 percent, because 1600 divided by the new 8000 is 0.20
options.misconception: divides the change by the value after the change

options.text: 25 percent, because 1600 divided by the new 8000 is 0.20 so the rate must be 25
options.misconception: reaches the right number through a wrong division

options.text: 80 percent, because 8000 divided by 6400 is 1.25 so the rate is 80
options.misconception: reports the new value as a percentage of the old value

questions.explanation: A percent change is the change divided by the starting value, so 8000 minus 6400 gives a change of 1600 residents, and 1600 over 6400 is 0.25, which is 25%. The alternative pair confirms it, because 8000 over 6400 is 1.25, meaning the new value is 125% of the old, and 125% minus 100% is 25%. Option B uses the wrong base, which always understates an increase.
questions.hint: Divide the change by the value from before the change.

questions.topic: Base used when a percent change is computed
questions.learningObjective: choose the correct base for a percent change
questions.stem: A sample of 45 grams grows to 54 grams. Which reading of that change is correct?

options.text: A 20% increase, using the 45 grams as the base
A 20% increase, using the 54 grams as the base
options.misconception: divides the 9 gram change by the weight after the change

options.text: A 16 and two thirds percent increase, using the 54 grams as the base
options.misconception: uses the final weight as the denominator and calls the result an increase

options.text: A 16 and two thirds percent increase, using the 45 grams as the base
options.misconception: computes the wrong rate but names the right base

Option C divides 9 by 54 and gets roughly 16.7%, which is correct arithmetic on the wrong base, and it describes the 45 gram weight as a percentage of the 54 gram one rather than the reverse.
questions.hint: The base for a percent change is the value before the change.

126 dollars, because the 35 dollar difference must be added on
options.misconception: confuses the percent with the missing amount of dollars

options.text: 122.85 dollars, because 91 multiplied by 0.35 is the size of the cut

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Which base a tip is calculated on
questions.learningObjective: explain how a change of base changes a percentage
questions.stem: A meal costs 45 dollars before tax. The tax rate is 18% and the restaurant adds a tip of 18% of the pre-tax meal price. Explain why quoting the tip as 18% of the tax-inclusive amount would give a different total, and show both totals in dollars.

answer.exemplar: A percent is a fraction of whatever base it is attached to, so changing the base changes the amount even though the rate is unchanged. The tax is 0.18 of 45 dollars, which is 8.10 dollars, making the tax-inclusive bill 45 plus 8.10, or 53.10 dollars. A tip of 18% of the pre-tax price is 0.18 of 45, which is 8.10 dollars, so the total is 53.10 plus 8.10, or 61.20 dollars. Quoting the tip against the tax-inclusive amount gives 0.18 of 53.10, which is 9.558 dollars, and the total becomes 53.10 plus 9.558, or 62.658 dollars. The two totals differ by 1.458 dollars, and the gap exists entirely because the larger base was used the second time. Quoting the base matters as much as quoting the rate.

questions.explanation: The stem fixes the rate at 18% and asks only which amount the rate is taken of, so the whole difference comes from the base. Working the pre-tax base gives 45 multiplied by 0.18, which is 8.10, and the tip-inclusive total is 61.20 dollars. Working the tax-inclusive base of 53.10 dollars gives 9.558, and the total is 62.658 dollars. The gap of 1.458 dollars is exactly 18% of the 8.10 dollars of tax, which is the cleanest way to see that the tax got taxed a second time.
questions.hint: Write both percentages against an explicit base before doing any arithmetic.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Negative exponents
questions.learningObjective: interpret a negative exponent
questions.stem: Which expression has the same value as 4 to the power minus 2?

options.text: 1 over 16, because a negative exponent counts factors of the base sent below the line
minus 8, because the power 2 is applied to the negative of 4
options.misconception: reads the minus sign as part of the base rather than the exponent

options.text: 16, because the negative sign has no effect on the value
options.misconception: believes a negative exponent can be removed without changing the result

options.text: 1 over 2, because a negative exponent halves the base
options.misconception: believes a negative exponent takes a square root of the base

questions.explanation: A positive exponent counts repeated multiplication, and 4 squared is 4 times 4, which is 16. A negative exponent sends those copies into the denominator, so 4 to the power minus 2 is 1 over 16, equal to 0.0625. The rule is that a to the power n and a to the power minus n are reciprocals, and the check is that their product is 1.
questions.hint: Count how many copies of the base go above or below the line.

questions.topic: Evaluating a negative exponent

questions.stem: Evaluate 5 to the power minus 3 and report the value as a decimal. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Three copies of 5 multiply to 5 times 5 times 5, which is 125, and a negative exponent puts those three copies in the denominator instead. questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Product rule for powers
questions.learningObjective: apply the product rule to like bases
questions.stem: Which expression has the same value as x to the fourth power times x to the sixth power?

options.text: x to the tenth power, because exponents add when like bases are multiplied
x to the twenty fourth power, because exponents multiply
options.misconception: applies the power of a power rule to a product of like bases

options.text: x squared, because exponents subtract when like bases are multiplied
options.misconception: applies the quotient rule to a product of like bases

options.text: x to the twelfth power, because the number of written terms is added
options.misconception: adds the exponents of the two terms plus a one for each factor

questions.explanation: Expanding the product literally gives ten copies of x altogether, since four plus six is ten, and ten copies of x is x to the tenth power. Writing the rule this way makes clear that the exponents add because the factors are being combined, not raised. The same expansion works for any numbers of copies, not only 4 and 6.
questions.hint: Count the copies of the base in the whole product.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Product and quotient of powers
questions.learningObjective: combine a product and a quotient of like bases
questions.stem: Simplify 2 to the sixth power times 2 to the fourth power, all divided by 2 to the third power. Report the value as a whole number.
questions.explanation: The product of the first two terms is 2 to the tenth power, since six plus four is ten, and dividing by 2 to the third power subtracts three, leaving 2 to the seventh power. Evaluating gives 128. The second route checks the same result by cancelling outright, since the 2 cubed in the denominator cancels three of the ten copies of 2 in the numerator, leaving seven copies.
questions.hint: Add the exponents, then subtract the exponent in the denominator.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Power of a power
questions.learningObjective: apply the power of a power rule
questions.stem: Which expression has the same value as the quantity x to the third power all raised to the fourth power?

options.text: x to the twelfth power, because the exponents multiply
x to the seventh power, because the exponents add
options.misconception: applies the product rule to a nested power

options.text: x to the eighty first power, because the base is raised twice
options.misconception: cubes the base and then the exponent without applying any rule

options.text: x to the one twelfth power, because the outer power divides the inner
options.misconception: believes a power in the exponent divides rather than multiplies

questions.explanation: Raising the quantity x cubed to the fourth power means four copies of x cubed, and each of those copies is three x values, so there are four times three, which is twelve, copies of x. The rule is that exponents multiply, and the reason is that repeated multiplication is being counted twice over. The same counting gives 2 to the tenth power for the quantity x squared raised to the fifth power.
questions.hint: Count the copies of x in the whole expression.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Exponent produced by a nested power
questions.learningObjective: find the base-exponent form of a nested power
questions.stem: The quantity 7 squared, all raised to the fifth power, is rewritten with base 7. What is the exponent in that form? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Seven squared raised to the fifth power means five copies of a quantity that holds two copies of 7, so there are 5 times 2, which is 10, copies of 7. That is 7 to the tenth power. The check is to evaluate both sides: 49 raised to the fifth power is the same number as 7 raised to 10, because 49 is 7 squared and five copies of it are ten copies of 7.
questions.hint: Multiply the inner exponent by the outer exponent.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Power of a product
questions.learningObjective: apply the power of a product rule
questions.stem: Which expression has the same value as the quantity 2y squared, all raised to the third power?

options.text: 8y to the sixth power, because each factor inside is raised to the outer power
6y to the fifth power, because the numbers 2 and 3 are added to the exponent
options.misconception: adds the coefficient and the exponent instead of raising each factor

options.text: 8y to the fifth power, because only the coefficient is raised to the outer power
options.misconception: raises the coefficient but leaves the exponent of y untouched

options.text: 2y to the sixth power, because the outer power reaches only the variable
options.misconception: leaves the coefficient outside while raising the variable alone

questions.explanation: Three copies of the quantity 2y squared give six copies of y and a coefficient of 2 cubed, which is 8, so the whole expression is 8y to the sixth power. The rule says every factor inside the bracket is raised to the outer power, which is the same reason that distributing a bracket multiplies each term. The check: substituting y equal to 2 into both sides gives the same value, 8 times 2 to the sixth power.
questions.hint: Raise the coefficient and the variable part separately.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Evaluating a power of a product
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a product raised to a power
questions.stem: Evaluate the quantity 2 multiplied by 3 squared, all raised to the third power. Report the value as a whole number.
questions.explanation: Inside the bracket 2 times 3 squared is 2 times 9, which is 18, and 18 cubed is 5832. The second route raises each factor separately: 2 cubed is 8 and 3 squared cubed is 3 to the sixth power, which is 729, so 8 times 729 is 5832. The two routes agree, which confirms that the outer power reaches every factor inside the bracket.
questions.hint: Either cube the whole bracket or raise each factor to the cube.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Rational exponent and its radical form
questions.learningObjective: match a rational exponent to a radical
questions.stem: Which radical form is equal to 5 raised to the power three halves?

options.text: The square root of 5 cubed
The cube root of 5 squared
options.misconception: reads the fraction the wrong way round, denominator for numerator

options.text: The square root of 5 squared
options.misconception: ignores the numerator of the exponent entirely

options.text: The fifth root of 3 squared
options.misconception: reads the base and the exponent as though they had traded places

questions.explanation: A rational exponent with denominator 2 asks for a square root, because dividing the count of copies by 2 halves them, and the numerator 3 says how many times to repeat that root. So 5 to the three halves is the square root of 5 cubed, which is the square root of 125. The check is the reciprocal identity, since raising that value to the two thirds power returns 5.
questions.hint: The denominator of the exponent chooses the root, the numerator chooses the count.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Evaluating a rational exponent
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a rational exponent
questions.stem: Evaluate 8 raised to the power two thirds and report the value. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The denominator 3 asks for a cube root, and the cube root of 8 is 2, so the expression is 2 squared, which is 4. The order matters: taking the two thirds of the power in the other order would give the square root of 8 cubed, which is the square root of 512, and that is not 4. So the value confirms the root was taken first.
questions.hint: Take the cube root of 8 first, then square the result.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Principal square root
questions.learningObjective: identify the principal square root
questions.stem: What is the principal square root of 169?

options.text: 13, because 13 multiplied by 13 is 169
169, because a root repeats the number it is taken of
options.misconception: believes the square root of a number equals the number

options.text: minus 13, because roots always come in negative pairs
options.misconception: believes the symbol by itself must name the negative root

options.text: 26, because the two roots of 169 are added together
options.misconception: adds the two roots instead of choosing between them

questions.explanation: The square root symbol names the nonnegative root, so for 169 it means 13, since 13 times 13 is 169. The negative root exists too, and the equation x squared equal to 169 has both 13 and minus 13 as solutions, but the symbol alone always means the positive one. This distinction is what makes later algebra predictable.
questions.hint: The square root symbol is nonnegative by definition.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Simplest radical form
questions.learningObjective: put a radical into simplest form
questions.stem: Which expression is the simplest form of the square root of 200?

options.text: 10 times the square root of 2
20 times the square root of 5
options.misconception: extracts a factor that is not a perfect square

options.text: 5 times the square root of 8
options.misconception: stops before removing every square factor from what is left

options.text: 100 times the square root of 2
options.misconception: moves the whole radicand out without leaving any root on it

questions.explanation: Factoring 200 as 100 times 2 lets the perfect square 100 come out as 10, leaving the square root of 2, which has no further square factor. Option C is equal to the same number but is not in simplest form, because 8 still contains a 4. Option D comes from treating the radicand itself as though it were its own square root, which is the slip that produces the largest wrong answer.
questions.hint: Pull out the largest perfect square you can, then check what is left.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Coefficient of a simplified radical
questions.learningObjective: report the outside factor of a simplified radical
questions.stem: The square root of 147 is written as a whole number times the square root of a number with no perfect square factor. What is that whole number? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Factoring 147 as 49 times 3 pulls the perfect square 49 out as 7, leaving the square root of 3, so the outside number is 7. The check is that 7 times 7 times 3 is 147. Choosing 3 instead of 7 would leave a radicand of 49 that is still a perfect square, so the form would not be finished and the outside number would be wrong.
questions.hint: Find the largest square that divides the radicand and take its root.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Adding radicals with unlike radicands
questions.learningObjective: add radicals by first matching radicands
questions.stem: Which expression is equal to 3 times the square root of 2 plus 2 times the square root of 8?

options.text: 7 times the square root of 2, because 2 times the square root of 8 is 4 times the square root of 2
5 times the square root of 10, because the two radicands multiply when the terms add
options.misconception: adds radicals by multiplying the radicands as though adding fractions

options.text: 6 times the square root of 4, because the coefficients and the radicands combine
options.misconception: combines both the numbers and the roots as if they were all like terms

options.text: 7 times the square root of 8, because the coefficients add without being simplified
options.misconception: adds the coefficients but leaves the second radical unreduced

questions.explanation: Radicals can only be added term by term when their radicands match, so the second term is rewritten first: 8 is 4 times 2, so 2 times the square root of 8 is 2 times 2 times the square root of 2, which is 4 times the square root of 2. The sum is then 3 plus 4, which is 7, times the square root of 2. Multiplying radicands, as in option B, is what division does, not addition.
questions.hint: Reduce each radical to the same radicand before adding the coefficients.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Quotient of two radicals
questions.learningObjective: divide two radicals and simplify
questions.stem: Find the value of the square root of 72 divided by the square root of 2. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The quotient of two radicals with the same index is the radical of the quotient, so this is the square root of 72 over 2, which is the square root of 36, which is 6. The second route is to reduce each radical first: the square root of 72 is 6 times the square root of 2, and dividing that by the square root of 2 leaves 6, since the square root of 2 cancels exactly.
questions.hint: Divide the radicands, then take the root of the result.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Rationalising a denominator
questions.learningObjective: clear a radical from a denominator
questions.stem: Four labelled steps describe writing a fraction that has a radical in its denominator in a form with no radical in the denominator. Put them in the order in which they must be carried out.

options.text: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same radical
Expand the denominator as a product of two equal radicals
Simplify the radical now sitting in the numerator
Cancel any common factor left in the fraction

questions.explanation: The first move must multiply top and bottom by the same radical, because that is the only way to change the denominator without changing the value. The new denominator is then a product of two equal radicals, which is a perfect square and so comes out as a whole number. Only then is it worth simplifying the numerator and cancelling, since earlier steps would just create work to undo.
questions.hint: Whatever you multiply by has to go on both the top and the bottom.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Value of a rationalised fraction
questions.learningObjective: read off the parts of a rationalised fraction
questions.stem: The fraction 3 over the square root of 12 is written as a times the square root of b over c, with b free of square factors. What is the value of a plus b plus c? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The square root of 12 is 2 times the square root of 3, so the fraction is 3 over 2 times the square root of 3. Multiplying top and bottom by the square root of 3 gives 3 times the square root of 3 over 6, and the 3 on top cancels against the 6 below, leaving the square root of 3 over 2. So the parts are 1, 3 and 2, and they add to 6. The value itself is about 0.866, which matches 3 over 3.464.
questions.hint: Reduce the denominator first, then multiply by the matching radical.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: The conjugate of a binomial
questions.learningObjective: identify the conjugate of a binomial with a radical
questions.stem: What is the conjugate of 4 plus 3 times the square root of 5?

options.text: 4 minus 3 times the square root of 5
4 plus 3 times the square root of 5, which is the binomial itself
options.misconception: believes the conjugate of an expression is the same expression

options.text: 3 times the square root of 5 minus 4, which reverses the order of the terms
options.misconception: believes the conjugate also swaps the two terms of the binomial

options.text: 4 minus 3 times 5, which drops the root and keeps the numbers
options.misconception: believes the conjugate removes the radical from the expression

questions.explanation: The conjugate of a two term expression is built by reversing the sign of the second term and leaving everything else alone. The sign flip is what makes the product tidy, because the square root then multiplies its own negative and vanishes. That is exactly why the conjugate is the tool used to clear a radical from a denominator.
questions.hint: Change the sign of the second term and leave the first alone.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Product of a binomial and its conjugate
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a product of conjugates
questions.stem: Multiply the quantity 5 plus the square root of 3 by the quantity 5 minus the square root of 3. What is the result? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: This is the pattern a squared minus b squared, with a equal to 5 and b equal to the square root of 3, so the product is 5 squared minus the square root of 3 squared, which is 25 minus 3, giving 22. The reason it works is that the cross terms are 5 times minus the square root of 3 and 5 times the square root of 3, which cancel each other exactly, leaving only the two square terms behind.
questions.hint: The cross terms cancel, so only the squares of each part survive.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solving a quadratic by taking square roots
questions.learningObjective: solve a quadratic equation by taking square roots
questions.stem: Four labelled steps describe solving a quadratic equation in which the squared term stands alone, by taking square roots. Put them in the order in which they must be carried out.

options.text: Isolate the squared term on one side with nothing else on that side
Take the square root of both sides and write both the positive and the negative root
Solve each resulting linear equation for the unknown
Check any candidate whose sign might not suit the original equation

questions.explanation: Taking a square root of a sum is not the same as adding the roots, so the squared term has to be on its own before anything is taken. Then both roots of each side are needed, since a squared equal to a positive number has two solutions, and the square root of a squared quantity is an absolute value rather than the quantity itself. The final check catches a candidate that failed because of its sign.
questions.hint: The squared term must be alone before you can take its root.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solution of a squared binomial
questions.learningObjective: solve a squared binomial equation
questions.stem: The equation the quantity 3x plus 2, all squared, equals 64. What is the positive solution for x? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Taking square roots of both sides gives 3x plus 2 equal to 8 or equal to minus 8. The first gives 3x equal to 6 and x equal to 2, and the second gives 3x equal to minus 10, so x is minus 10 over 3. Substituting x equal to 2 back in confirms it: 3 times 2 plus 2 is 8, and 8 squared is 64, so the positive solution is 2 and the negative one is not wanted here.
questions.hint: Take both roots of 64, then solve each resulting linear equation.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Extraneous roots from squaring
questions.learningObjective: explain why squaring can add a solution
questions.stem: Squaring both sides of a radical equation can produce a solution the original equation does not have. What must always be checked afterwards?

options.text: Every candidate solution in the original unsquared equation
Whether the squared equation has a repeated root
options.misconception: believes a repeated root is the sign that squaring changed the solution set

options.text: Whether each candidate is a whole number
options.misconception: believes only integer candidates need verifying

options.text: Whether the coefficient of the candidate is positive
options.misconception: checks the sign of a coefficient rather than the value of the candidate

questions.explanation: Squaring is a one way move, because 3 and minus 3 both square to 9, so the squared equation is satisfied by values the original rejects. The only defence is to substitute every candidate back into the original equation and discard the ones that fail. A candidate that fails usually fails because the original root demanded a nonnegative value and the candidate is negative.
questions.hint: Substitute each candidate back into the equation you started with.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Candidates that fail a radical equation
questions.learningObjective: count candidates rejected by a radical equation
questions.stem: Squaring the equation the square root of the quantity 2x minus 3 equals the quantity x minus 3 gives the candidates x equal to 2 and x equal to 6. How many of those candidates fail the original equation? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: At x equal to 2 the left side is the square root of 1, which is 1, while the right side is 2 minus 3, which is minus 1, so that candidate fails. At x equal to 6 the left side is the square root of 9, which is 3, and the right side is 6 minus 3, which is 3, so that one holds. Exactly one candidate is rejected, and it is the smaller one, which is typical because a root is nonnegative.
questions.hint: Evaluate both sides of the original equation at each candidate.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Domain of a square root rule
questions.learningObjective: find the domain of a rule containing a square root
questions.stem: A rule is written as the square root of the quantity 7 minus x. Which set of inputs does it accept?

options.text: All real x with x less than or equal to 7
All real x with x greater than or equal to 7
options.misconception: reverses the inequality when isolating x inside the root

options.text: All real x, because a root of any number is defined
options.misconception: believes a square root exists for negative inputs as well

options.text: Only the single value x equal to 7
options.misconception: believes the input must make the quantity under the root exactly zero

questions.explanation: The square root function is only defined when the quantity under the root is zero or more, so 7 minus x must be at least zero, which means x is at most 7. Every real x below 7 is fine because the quantity is then positive. Options B and D both narrow the set incorrectly, and the domain is a whole interval rather than a single point.
questions.hint: The quantity under the root has to be zero or more.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Effect of a cube root on sign
questions.learningObjective: take a cube root of a negative value
questions.stem: What is the cube root of minus 64?

options.text: Minus 4, because the cube of a negative number is negative
Plus 8, because roots never return a negative value
options.misconception: believes every root is nonnegative, which holds only for even indices

options.text: Minus 8, because the index 3 is carried over as the answer
options.misconception: believes the index is the value rather than the count of factors

options.text: Undefined, because negatives under roots are always forbidden
options.misconception: extends the rule about square roots to roots of odd index

questions.explanation: A cube root undoes three copies of a number, and three negative copies multiply to a negative result, so the cube root of minus 64 is minus 4. This is the key difference from a square root, which cannot accept a negative input because no square is negative. Any odd-indexed root keeps the sign of the quantity under it.
questions.hint: Ask how many copies of the base there are, then check the sign.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: A reduction checked by cross products
questions.learningObjective: verify a fraction reduction with cross products
questions.stem: A student reduces the fraction 45 over 63 to 5 over 7 by dividing both parts by 9. Which check on the cross products confirms the two fractions have the same value?

options.text: 45 times 7 and 63 times 5 are both 315, so the two ratios agree
45 times 7 and 63 times 5 are both 108, so the two ratios agree
options.misconception: reads the cross products as the sums of the parts rather than their products

options.text: 45 and 5 are both multiples of 5, so the two ratios agree
options.misconception: treats a shared factor as proof that the two fractions are equal

options.text: 63 and 7 are both multiples of 7, so the two ratios agree
options.misconception: checks only the denominators and never compares the two cross products

questions.explanation: Two fractions are equal exactly when their cross products are equal, and here 45 times 7 is 315 while 63 times 5 is also 315, so the reduction kept the value. The alternative check is the decimal route: 45 over 63 is five sevenths, which is about 0.714, and 5 over 7 is about 0.714 as well. Option B uses the sum 108, which is what the two parts add to and says nothing about the ratio.
questions.hint: Compare the two products formed by crossing the parts.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Percent rate used as a multiplier
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a percent error
questions.stem: A student must find an 18% tip on a bill of 84 dollars, multiplies 84 by 1.18, and reports 99.12 dollars as the tip. What has gone wrong?

options.text: The 0.18 rate should have been taken of the 84 dollars, giving a tip of 15.12 dollars
The 1.18 multiplier should have been applied to a subtotal that already included tax
options.misconception: moves the error to the tax rather than to the wrong multiplier

options.text: The rate should have been taken of 99.12 dollars rather than of 84 dollars
options.misconception: keeps the wrong multiplier and then re-takes the rate from the answer

options.text: The 84 dollars should have been doubled before the rate was applied
options.misconception: inflates the base by doubling it instead of choosing the right rate

questions.explanation: The number 1.18 already contains the original amount, so multiplying 84 by it gives the bill after the tip, not the tip. The tip on its own is 0.18 of 84, which is 15.12 dollars, and 84 plus 15.12 returns the 99.12 the student found. The diagnosis is a percent error of type one: a multiplier that includes the base has been used where a rate was needed.
questions.hint: Ask whether 84 is still present in the number that was produced.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Distributing a negative sign over a sum
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a sign error in distribution
questions.stem: A student must solve minus 2 multiplied by the quantity x plus 3, set equal to 10, writes minus 2x plus 3 equals 10, and reports x equal to 3.5. What has gone wrong?

options.text: The minus outside the bracket must reach both terms, giving minus 2x minus 6 equals 10 and x equal to minus 8
The 3 inside the bracket should have been doubled, giving minus 2x plus 6 equals 10
options.misconception: doubles the constant instead of applying the outside sign to it

options.text: The bracket should have been removed by dividing each term by the minus 2 in front
options.misconception: removes a bracket by dividing where it should be multiplied

options.text: The 10 on the right should first have been divided by the minus 2 to make it positive
options.misconception: changes the right side to tidy the left rather than distributing correctly

questions.explanation: The minus sign sits in front of the whole bracket, so it has to be shared by both terms inside, giving minus 2x minus 6. That equation gives minus 2x equal to 16, so x is minus 8, and substituting back gives minus 2 times minus 5, which is 10 as required. Distributing only to the first term is the classic sign slip in this topic.
questions.hint: Count how many terms the minus sign has to reach.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Taking a square root of both sides
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a square root error
questions.stem: A student must solve the equation x squared equal to 49, takes a square root of each side, writes x equal to 49, and stops there. What is the error?

options.text: The square root of x squared is the absolute value of x, so x is plus or minus 7
The square root of 49 is 7, so the student should have written x equal to 7
options.misconception: blames the arithmetic on 49 while accepting that only one root was taken

options.text: Both sides needed to be squared again to remove the root
options.misconception: believes squaring removes a root rather than introducing one

options.text: The 49 should have been divided by the coefficient of x squared first
options.misconception: believes a hidden coefficient of 1 must be removed before the root

questions.explanation: Taking a square root of each side reduces the equation to the absolute value of x equal to 7, and that is solved by two values, 7 and minus 7. The student both kept the radicand instead of taking its root and reported only one of the two solutions. The general rule is that the root of a squared quantity is the absolute value of that quantity, not the quantity itself.
questions.hint: Reduce the left side to an absolute value before solving it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Extracting a factor from a radical
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a radical simplification error
questions.stem: A student must write the square root of 75 in simplest form, factors 75 as 3 times 25, pulls the 3 out, and reports 3 times the square root of 25. What has gone wrong?

options.text: Only a perfect square comes out from under a radical, so 75 equals 25 times 3 gives 5 times the square root of 3
The factors of 75 should be added rather than multiplied, giving 3 times the square root of 28
options.misconception: adds the two factors together instead of multiplying them into the radicand

options.text: The whole radicand can be taken out, so 3 times the square root of 25 becomes 75 times the square root of 1
options.misconception: moves the entire radicand outside without taking a root of it

options.text: The 3 was treated as though it were a square, so the radicand should have been left as 75
options.misconception: pulls a number out of a radical when that number is not a square

questions.explanation: Only a perfect square may be brought outside a radical, and of the two factors here it is 25, not 3, that qualifies, so the form is 5 times the square root of 3. Pulling the 3 out leaves 25 under the root, which is still a perfect square, so the job is unfinished. The check is to square the outside number and multiply by what remains, which gives 25 times 3, or 75 as required.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two factors is itself a perfect square.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Why a fall and rise of the same size do not cancel
questions.learningObjective: explain the compounding of two opposite percents
questions.stem: Explain why a price reduced by 20% and then increased by 20% does not return to its starting value, and state the net percent change from the original.

answer.exemplar: The two percentages act on two different amounts, because the first is a fraction of the original price and the second is a fraction of the smaller price that the first step produced. Let the original price be 100 dollars. The 20% reduction leaves 80 dollars, since 20% of 100 is 20. The 20% increase is now taken from 80 dollars, and 20% of 80 is 16, so the price ends at 96 dollars. Ninety six is 4% below 100, so the net change is a 4% decrease. The reason the two percentages do not cancel is that 20% of 100 is 20 while 20% of 80 is only 16, a difference of 4, and that 4 is exactly the shortfall. The general pattern is that a fall of r percent followed by a rise of r percent leaves the price multiplied by 0.8 times 1.2, which is 0.96, so the net change is a decrease of 4 percent for any rate r, found from the product of one minus r and one plus r, which is one minus r squared. The general lesson is that a later percentage always uses the amount current at that moment, so reversing direction changes the base as well as the rate.

questions.explanation: The stem asks for a net change, and the whole of it is decided by which amount each percentage is taken of. Taking both from 100 makes them cancel, which is the tempting error. Computing 0.8 times 1.2 as 0.96 shows the true multiplier, and 1 minus 0.96 is 0.04, so the price sits 4% below where it started. Stating the general case, one minus r times one plus r is one minus r squared, which is what makes the shortfall always a decrease of r squared as a percent.
questions.hint: Track what amount the second percentage is taken from.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Deciding termination from prime factors
questions.learningObjective: explain the terminating decimal test
questions.stem: Explain how the prime factorisation of the denominator of a reduced fraction decides whether its decimal expansion terminates or repeats, and give one terminating and one repeating example.

answer.exemplar: A reduced fraction a over b has a terminating expansion exactly when b has no prime factor other than 2 and 5, and the reason is that a terminating decimal is always a whole number of tenths, hundredths or thousandths, so its denominator divides a power of 10, and 10 factors as 2 times 5. For example 1 over 8 reduces with a denominator of 8, which is 2 cubed, so the decimal is 0.125 and stops after three places. By contrast 1 over 12 has a denominator of 12, which is 2 squared times 3, and that 3 is not a factor of 10, so the expansion repeats: 0.0833 and so on. The size of the factor 3 does not matter, since no amount of tens can absorb it. Working through the general case, a denominator of 2 to the a times 5 to the b is cleared by multiplying the fraction by enough tens to make the exponents match, and any other prime survives forever, forcing a repeating block. The length of the terminating expansion is then the larger of a and b, so a denominator with a high power of 2 needs more places to clear. The test therefore settles the question in one look at the denominator and requires no long division at all.

questions.explanation: The stem asks for the mechanism, and the mechanism is that a terminating decimal always has a denominator built from the primes in 10. Examples settle the claim: 1 over 8 terminates because 8 is a power of 2, and 1 over 12 repeats because 12 carries a 3. The general case shows the test is decisive, because a surviving prime cannot be absorbed by any power of 10.
questions.hint: Compare the primes in the denominator with the primes in 10.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: The zero exponent
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a zero exponent
questions.stem: What is the value of 9 to the power zero?

options.text: 1, because any nonzero number to the power zero is 1
0, because raising to a power always shrinks the base
options.misconception: believes a zero exponent drives the value to zero

options.text: 9, because a zero exponent leaves the base unchanged
options.misconception: believes a zero exponent means no power is applied

options.text: Undefined, because zero exponents are not permitted
options.misconception: believes the rule excludes the case of a zero power

questions.explanation: An exponent counts repeated multiplication, and zero copies of anything multiply to the empty product, which is 1 by convention. The rule follows from the fact that dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal, so a to the power zero must undo a to the power one. The value 0 to the power zero is left undefined, but any nonzero base raised to the zero power is 1.
questions.hint: Ask how many copies of the base are being multiplied together.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Why squaring adds a solution
questions.learningObjective: explain the source and the removal of an extraneous root
questions.stem: Explain why squaring both sides of a radical equation can produce a solution the original equation does not have, and describe the check that removes it.

answer.exemplar: Squaring is not reversible, because two different values can share a square. The value 3 and the value minus 3 both square to 9, so a squared equation is satisfied by both, while the equation with a square root in it may accept only one of them. That is the whole reason squaring a radical equation can produce an extra candidate: the squared form has lost the sign information the root was carrying. The same thing happens with the positive root, because the square root of a squared quantity is the absolute value of that quantity rather than the quantity itself, so a negative input can look like a solution after squaring and fail on substitution. The check is therefore mechanical and complete: write down every candidate the squared equation gives, then substitute each one back into the original equation with the radical still in place, and discard any candidate for which the two sides do not agree exactly. Working the square root of the quantity 2x minus 3 equal to the quantity x minus 3 shows the pattern, since squaring gives the two candidates 2 and 6, and substituting 2 gives a left side of 1 against a right side of minus 1, so 2 is rejected while 6 survives. Testing candidates is not optional, because the squared equation is a weaker statement than the original and the only way to recover the original is to go back to it.

questions.explanation: The stem asks for the mechanism and the remedy, and both are about lost sign information. Squaring merges a value and its negative, so the squared equation is weaker than the original, and only substituting back into the original can separate the two. The worked pair 2 and 6 shows the check rejecting the smaller candidate because 1 does not equal minus 1.
questions.hint: Ask what information squaring throws away, then test each candidate in the original.
